highlights.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
highlights.summary: Philadelphia police said the tip was "flagged as spam", but criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.
body: An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.
Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.
points: Philadelphia police said the tip was "flagged as spam", but criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

highlights.title: Anthropic’s AI gave Philadelphia police a fake tip about an unsolved homicide
highlights.summary: An Anthropic AI model provided false information about an unsolved homicide to a Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tipline, according to a report from 6abc. In a statement released on Friday, the PPD said the AI model sent the tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18th, but the…
body: The false tip ‘purported to come from someone who might have information about the case.’

Anthropic learned its AI model sent the false tip on September 28th and notified the PPD on October 7th. The company said that during testing, its AI model was interacting with “randomly selected websites” and submitted false information through the PPD’s tipline, according to the PPD’s statement. The submission “purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.

After discovering the submission, Anthropic halted the testing process that led to the false tip. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google have been the subject of increased scrutiny after disclosing that their AI models escaped testing environments and hacked third-party companies. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, advocated for slowing down the development of AI in response to these incidents.
Anthropic also notes in its report that “Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”

highlights.title: 'You will see me back' - Smith vows 2027 return after Swiss Darts Trophy win
highlights.summary: Former world champion Michael Smith says he plans on "playing 100 per cent of the tournaments" in 2027 after an opening win at the Swiss Darts Trophy.
body: 'Bully Boy' Smith fought back from 3-1 down to beat Rob Owen, hitting 50 per cent of his doubles in just his fourth European Tour event of the season.
"I've missed this. I want to apologise and also make a promise in 2027 I will be playing 100 per cent of the tournaments. You will see me back," said the 2023 world champion.
Smith is chasing down the final spots in the European Championship race and the St Helens thrower beat Owen 6-4 to set up a meeting with Jermaine Wattimena for a place in Sunday's action.

Rob Cross was Friday's standout performer for the second event in a row, averaging 105.95 in his 6-3 success against Mario Vandenbogaerde and will take on Luke Woodhouse on the back of his brilliant opening round performance at the World Grand Prix.

highlights.title: Persona’s Horrifying Dong Monster Will Haunt My Nightmares Forever
highlights.summary: Atlus’s Persona series of role-playing games incorporates a huge variety of mythological and folkloric creatures from around the world. Some are formidable warriors like Odin from Norse mythology or the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
body: No, your eyes aren’t playing tricks on you. That is a giant, green penis with four arms, multiple tentacles, and a gaping mouth. He is a demon weiner, ribbed for your psychic displeasure. And yes, he’s riding a golden chariot. Mara is a Buddhist demon associated with temptation, lust, and earthly pleasures. The name is borrowed from Sanskrit, where it means "the Destroyer" or "the Evil One." It’s also a visual pun, because in Japanese “mara” is slang for “penis,” though he’s not depicted this way anywhere else in pop culture.

The tubular terror was slated to appear in 2024’s Metaphor ReFantazio, but was mercifully cut from the final version of the game, presumably to get that T for Teen ESRB rating. He has consistently been one of the most popular demons in the series, even claiming the number-one spot in an official 2017 Atlus poll.

highlights.title: AI Can Cut Film Budgets by Up to 40%, Says ‘The Outlaws’ Director Kang Yoon-sung, as Netflix Reveals Use on 300 Titles: ‘A Human Touch Is Absolutely Essential’
highlights.summary: Netflix has used AI in one form or another on some 300 of its titles, Lee Sung-gyun, the streamer’s senior director of APAC production, told an audience at the Busan International Film Festival.
body: On the same panel, “The Outlaws” director Kang Yoon-sung said AI workflows could take 30% to 40% off a feature film’s production budget.

Lee said new technology has always startled people when it arrives. “All these technological changes and new tools have helped a great deal with the ‘how,’ how we make what we make better, but they never decided the ‘why,’ why we have to tell this story,” he said. “AI is the same.”

He also screened a reel from Eyeline, Netflix’s VFX studio, about what the company calls hybrid production, which mixes live-action photography, VFX and generative tools. A second clip showed AI and VFX together producing large crowd scenes for the Netflix India title “Glory.” Lee said that under tight budgets and schedules, those scenes would normally have had to be dropped.

highlights.title: ‘They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones’: Peter Crome’s best phone picture
highlights.summary: The photographer was walking home in London when he caught the attention of a pair of canine snoops. Walking home after dropping his little girl at school, Peter Crome sensed he was being watched.
body: The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”

Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison. He crossed the road to draw their attention, then took a single photo on his iPhone 14 Pro. “This is the sort of picture I would have sent my mum before she passed away a couple of years ago. I think this one would have really tickled her,” Crome says.

body: It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.
It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.
The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.
After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

highlights.title: Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting
highlights.summary: Workers at three major publishing houses tell WIRED that LLMs are being used for publicity, cover art, back cover copy, and emails, as some execs push junior staff to champion the tech.
body: In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.

According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.

At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body —are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.

highlights.title: Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
highlights.summary: The new image isn’t just stunning—it may also provide clues about how this star survived its own explosion.
body: Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.

Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.

highlights.title: ‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop
highlights.summary: "Staggering." "Overwhelming." "Unprecedented." "Surreal." "Pure insanity." Those were among the descriptions more than three dozen mathematicians reached for in conversations with The Verge as they tried to make sense of the flood of mathematical results OpenAI abruptly dropped on the field this…
body: Careers upended overnight, academics will have to separate solutions from slop while OpenAI moves on.

In all, OpenAI released nearly 400 AI-generated results. These were spread across more than 700 manuscripts and covered a diverse array of mathematical disciplines, including combinatorics, several branches of geometry, number theory, theoretical computer science, algebra, topology, probability and statistical mechanics, and mathematical physics. The collection is so vast that OpenAI felt the need to publish guidance on how to navigate the sprawling GitHub repository.

The sheer volume of work makes even a preliminary assessment as to exactly what the company has released difficult. In the hours and days following the drop, most mathematicians The Verge spoke with said they were still struggling to digest everything; several said that simply working through the roughly 40-page table of contents and abstracts took them the better part of an hour. “Just going over the entire list of abstracts is overwhelming,” said Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a professor of mathematics at the University of Connecticut.

highlights.summary: Avatar: Seven Havens is a far more mystery-driven series than its predecessors, The Legend of Korra and Avatar: The Last Airbender. Avatar Korra supposedly caused a cataclysm that destroyed most of the world, but it’s unclear why she would do that and how the new Avatar might be able to fix things.
body: This article contains spoilers for the first episode of Avatar: Seven Havens.

In the series premiere, “On the Horizon,” Ellora — the Haven where this season takes place — celebrates a festival to mark its founding in the wake of the cataclysm. The actors in a play explaining the history are dressed in a rainbow of colors. Those colors also appear in charts of the seven chakras. An overhead image of Ellora shows the Haven of Wind and Sand appears to be made of red-hued rocks, the color associated with the root chakra. “The Root Chakra” is also the name of the season finale.

The Avatar franchise is based on Buddhist mysticism, following the cycle of reincarnation that Aang, Korra, and the new Avatars Pavi (Saheli Khan) and Nisha (Aishu Devan) are all part of. Series co-creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko previously dove into chakras as a meditation aid in the Avatar: The Last Airbender season 2 episode “The Guru,” when Guru Pathik trained Aang to cleanse blockages from his seven chakras in order to gain control over the Avatar State.

highlights.title: Spa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont Blanc
highlights.summary: An autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descend. Mont Blanc is hiding behind the clouds, but the Aiguille du Midi spears the sky above a mountainside ablaze with russet, gold and tawny…
body: Our little group has trundled up to Mont Lachat station (altitude: 2,115 metres) on the Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs improbably steep slopes from the French alpine town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. Operational since 1909, the railway was once intended to reach the 4,809-metre summit of Mont Blanc, but war, glacial terrain and waning funds put an end to that ambition. But even from Mont Lachat, the view is a showstopper. On one side, the Bionnassay Glacier slips scenically down the slope, a buzzard soaring over the milky-green glacial lake at its base, while on the other the Chamonix valley basks in soft autumnal sunshine.

Autumn is golden season in the Alps, when you can find quieter hiking trails, lower prices and air crisp enough to stir the senses without nipping your fingers. Once focused purely on winter sports, the region’s resorts have spent years building up their summer credentials to offer hiking and biking through flower-strewn meadows. Now they’re marketing their shoulder season, too, to meet a growing demand for off-peak escapes.

highlights.title: How This Tiny Startup Built the World’s Safest Bike Helmet
highlights.summary: Inspired by head-banging woodpeckers, Vancouver-based Pikio Labs has discovered a new approach to skull protection.
body: For decades, researchers judged cycling helmets on how well they protected against direct impacts. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission ( CPSC ) still does, even though research shows the danger isn't just how hard your head hits the ground, but how violently it twists. That rotational movement can make the brain twist and stretch inside the skull, increasing the risk of concussion and other brain injuries.

Not waiting for the CPSC to catch up, the cycling industry got to work. Multidirectional Impact Protection System, or MIPS, hit the market in 2007 and is now a common feature on premium helmets. At the same time, Virginia Tech turned helmet safety into something of a competition for manufacturers. In 2018, it launched helmet STAR ratings (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk), testing beyond the legal minimum and measuring both linear and rotational impacts.

Only four of the first 30 helmets earned five stars, but by 2025, 167 of 272 achieved five stars, and Virginia Tech had to tighten its grading. That only drove competition and improved helmet technology. Suddenly, hitting the number one spot was good for business and brains.

highlights.title: Busan Market Chief Ellen Y.D. Kim Plots Year-Round ACFM 365 Platform, Warns Public Funding Has Stalled
highlights.summary: The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) should grow beyond its four days in Busan into a platform that runs all year, director Ellen Y.D. Kim tells Variety. She adds that public money for the market has not grown alongside it. Kim calls the idea ACFM 365.
body: “The biggest obstacle is funding,” Kim says. “The scale and the role of the market have grown quickly, but public support has not kept pace. National funding for ACFM has stayed at the same level for two years running. The film industry is small in scale, but it is the front-runner that opens the way for other industries. Supporting film is an investment, not a subsidy, and a market needs to be understood as industry infrastructure, not as an event.”

ACFM is in its 21st edition this year. Last year, industry registration rose 14.4% and overall attendance rose 13.5%. This year there are 339 exhibiting companies and institutions from 32 countries and territories, 17% more than last year. Tech exhibitors went from seven to 18, and national agencies and film commissions from 62 to 79. Thailand, the market’s first Country of Honor, has 28 exhibitors. Japan, the ProducerHub Focus Country, has 46.

highlights.title: Tim Dowling: at last I join the ranks of competent people
highlights.summary: It’s not often I get the chance to admire my handiwork, but I have finally fixed a light switch. For a single strange moment, everything appears to be in hand: the garden is tidy and free of dead branches, thanks to Gardening Steve; the back door, which refused to close properly for most of the…
body: The bathtub’s clawed feet are sitting on two long planks, safely spreading its enormous load evenly across the squishy, sinking bathroom floor. There are, theoretically, further repairs to be undertaken here, but I’ve reached an age where I’ve had to make sharp adjustments to my idea of what constitutes a permanent solution. If nothing else happens, this will do.

The kitchen table has been sanded down and refinished, by me. At first the effect was a bit too orangey for my wife’s liking, but over the subsequent days the colour of the wood seemed to improve when contrasted with the prospect of doing the whole thing all over again.
As the nights draw in, only one real job remains: the kitchen’s three-button dimmer switch wall plate is broken – one of the main lights simply won’t come on.
“If you can find a like-for-like replacement for the switch plate, I can put it in,” I say, still more rashly.

highlights.title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
highlights.summary: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase. The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and…
body: Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.

highlights.title: 5 Brilliant Anime That Don’t Waste a Single Episode
highlights.summary: Subjective taste inevitably plays a role here. A contemplative series like Mushi-shi and a sprawling space opera like Legend of the Galactic Heroes offer radically different versions of great storytelling.
body: Even the greatest anime usually have an episode or two that fans are tempted to skip during a rewatch. A select few, however, never let up. Every chapter advances the story, reveals something meaningful about its characters, or delivers an unforgettable display of animation.

The best anime balance compelling storytelling, striking visuals, and genuine thematic depth, but very few sustain that combination from beginning to end. Universally acclaimed series like Cowboy Bebop and Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood set an intimidating standard with their complex characters, carefully constructed worlds, and coherent themes. But plenty of less obvious choices come remarkably close to perfection.

The term “masterpiece” gets thrown around too easily, but it feels appropriate for Naoki Urasawa’s Monster. Madhouse’s 74-episode adaptation patiently unravels the manga’s philosophical mysteries without sacrificing the tension of its central game of cat and mouse.

highlights.title: Post-its, homework breaks and karaoke: inside the Women’s Pro Baseball League’s debut season
highlights.summary: The first league of its kind in 70 years brought players from all around the world to Illinois for eight weeks, writing a new chapter in the history of women’s sports.
body: On the morning of 14 September, Rocky Henley sat at her rental home’s dining room table amid scattered rulebooks, colorful markers and graph paper. The New York Heights manager drew a chart on a large poster – her method of sketching plays for the evening’s playoff game. Her assistant manager, Jackson, trudged in from the kitchen in flannel pajama pants and a Heights hoodie and watched her work. He also happens to be her son.

The Women’s Pro Baseball League (WPBL) is the first league of its kind in 70 years. Players hailed from across the US and 11 different countries to play for four teams: the Heights, Boston Hunters, San Francisco Firebells and Los Angeles Queens. While each team’s namesake city was selected for their market value and reputations for sports fandom, the eight-week inaugural season was played in entirety in Springfield, Illinois.
The inaugural season of the WPBL marked a pivotal moment in the women’s sports history books. The players, coaches and crew fashioned the paper, the pen and the ink to write this new chapter.

highlights.summary: The rising Korean actress brings her acclaimed American indie romance with Son Sukku to Busan, where she’s also serving on the festival’s main competition jury led by Chinese filmmaking legend Zhang Yimou.
body: Indie drama Bedford Park might just prove to be Korean actress Moon Choi’s big break in the U.S. film industry — but she’s nonetheless a little apprehensive about how it will play for the fans who know her work best.

Written and directed by first-time feature filmmaker Stephanie Ahn, Bedford Park stars Choi as Audrey, a 36-year-old Brooklyn physical therapist whose mother’s car accident summons her back to the suburban New Jersey home she has never quite escaped emotionally. The other driver is Eli (rising Korean star Son Sukku of The Roundup and D.P. fame), a prickly former wrestler and Korean adoptee raised by a neglectful white mother.

When Audrey visits Eli to share insurance info, the encounter descends into a heated argument over who was responsible for the crash. Their second meeting takes a harrowing turn when Audrey suffers a miscarriage on Eli’s doorstep. Soon, a bond begins to emerge between the two, as they glimpse a kindred spirit hidden beneath each other’s self-defenses. But their intimacy is messy and hard-won, more a meeting of two wounded Asian American survivors and strivers than the typical meet-cute of Korean romances.

highlights.title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US
highlights.summary: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen. On 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Biden commuted the life sentence of Leonard Peltier, after…
body: Outside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set to premiere just a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.

When it did, while the cameras rolled, the line of supporters erupted in joy for a commutation that allowed Peltier to serve the rest of his consecutive life sentences on house arrest, though it did not pardon him – not quite justice, but a victory so uncertain and so hard-fought, over more than half a lifetime, that I have cried every time I’ve rewatched it.
